When Anthropic lands in your ETF: Nasdaq-100 entry expected on 21 December, MSCI may move faster

meldungen.titel: Consulting Deep Dive, part 5: Roland Berger, Europe's home-grown strategy house and its turn towards restructuring
meldungen.text:
Roland Berger is the one top-tier strategy consultancy that was not born in America. Its founder, Roland Berger, spent five years at the Boston Consulting Group before setting up on his own in Munich in 1967. Nearly six decades later the firm remains a partnership headquartered in Germany, and it has just had the best year in its history: revenue of 1.01 billion euros in 2025, according to the firm. In Lünendonk's 2026 ranking of German consultancies it tops the table with 1,013.1 million euros, up 3.9 %, ahead of every other German-headquartered strategy firm. For perspective, Lünendonk puts the combined worldwide revenue of the German top 20 at 3.96 billion euros, with roughly 17,170 staff.

What drove the growth tells you where the work is. The firm itself credits projects on integrating AI, digitising processes and optimising supply chains, and the strongest regional gains came from Asia (plus 19 %) and the Americas (plus 11 %). Lünendonk's verdict on the wider market is blunter: consolidation rather than growth, with AI and restructuring as the two revenue engines. Roland Berger has leaned into the second. Since November 2025 a newly created unit, Ralf Schmitz CRO Management, has been placing seasoned Chief Restructuring Officers inside struggling companies to run turnaround programmes themselves rather than merely advise on them. That is a meaningful shift from slide decks to operational accountability, and it fits a German industrial base under pressure from energy costs, Chinese competition and the transition in automotive.

The firm's reputation rests on exactly that base: automotive, industrial goods, engineering and the Mittelstand. Its Transaction Services practice advises international industrial groups, mid-sized companies and private equity houses on deals, and a dedicated Private Equity and Strategic Investors practice publishes an annual European Private Equity Outlook; in the 2026 edition, three quarters of surveyed investors expected more private-equity M&A than in 2025. Job postings for its investor-support teams ask for several years in private equity, M&A, performance improvement or commercial due diligence, which shows the skills the firm prizes there.

Career guides describe the familiar ladder: Junior Consultant, Consultant, Senior Consultant, Project Manager, Principal and Partner (the firm does not publish an official version). Headcount estimates range widely, from about 2,400 to more than 4,600 depending on source and year, so treat any single number with caution.

On exits, the coaching site Hacking the Case Interview identifies seven typical paths: corporate strategy at European industrial companies, private equity, restructuring and interim management, start-ups, other strategy firms, business school and the public sector, with most consultants leaving between their second and sixth year. The private-equity route exists but is narrow; the same guides call it highly competitive, with only a small share making the jump. Alumni of the PE practice more often surface as operating partners, in portfolio-company leadership or in corporate development. The distinctive Roland Berger exit is therefore the industrial one: a strategy or transformation role at a large German manufacturer, or, increasingly, interim and restructuring work, where the new CRO unit gives consultants a direct line of sight.

None of the sources consulted publishes school-level hiring data. Given the firm's German-speaking core, HSG and WHU in your set are the obvious feeder schools, and HEC fits its Paris office, but that is inference rather than published fact.
meldungen.quelle: Roland Berger, press release on 2025 results

meldungen.titel: Oliver Wyman buys Synpulse, a Swiss financial-services tech consultancy, to bulk up its AI practice
meldungen.text:
Oliver Wyman, the consulting arm of Marsh McLennan, agreed on 19 November to acquire Synpulse, a consultancy founded in Switzerland in 1996 that advises banks, insurers and wealth managers on strategy, design, technology implementation and operations. Terms were not disclosed; the deal is expected to close in early 2027, subject to regulatory approval. Synpulse's roughly 1,200 employees will keep working from its offices across North America, Europe and Asia.

The two firms are hardly strangers: they have already run several end-to-end transformations for clients with combined teams. Oliver Wyman's chief executive, Ted Moynihan, framed the deal around Synpulse's "responsible AI" approach, which he said should help clients bring products to market more efficiently. It extends a steady run of bolt-ons, after the payments consultancy Innopay in 2024 and the healthcare analytics business Validate Health in 2025.

The pattern matters beyond this deal. Strategy houses are buying implementation capacity because AI projects are won and delivered on technology rather than slide decks, and financial services, Oliver Wyman's historic core, is where that pressure is most acute.

meldungen.titel: An Anthropic mathematician says he has proved the Riemann hypothesis with Claude, the most famous open problem in mathematics
meldungen.text:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, claims to have solved the Riemann hypothesis, first posed in 1859 and concerned with how the zeros of a particular function govern the distribution of prime numbers. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize problems, each carrying a one-million-dollar bounty from the Clay Mathematics Institute. In a statement on his website, Alpöge writes that he has, "working with Claude, discovered a proof", that the method extends to the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis, and that he and Claude have formalised the argument without assumptions in Lean, the proof-checking language.

The caveats are substantial. The proof has been published only on his website and has not been independently verified. Anthropic itself has neither commented nor taken part in the announcement; in August the company said it was working on the problem with Claude but did not expect those techniques to lead to a proof. Alpöge says he texted chief executive Dario Amodei late on Sunday night and appears to have held back publication until after Thursday's IPO. Under the Clay Institute's rules, a solution must be published and survive at least two years of scrutiny, winning general acceptance among mathematicians, before the prize can be considered.

The claim lands amid a broader upheaval in mathematics. Only one Millennium problem, the Poincaré conjecture, has ever been officially solved. In September OpenAI claimed to have cracked Navier-Stokes, deploying some 10,000 agents at a cost of millions; the result is widely thought credible but is clouded by allegations that it drew on unpublished work, which OpenAI denies. Alpöge had himself been working on Navier-Stokes with the NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, and in July he said he had solved the Jacobian conjecture using Claude.

meldungen.titel: Apple is quietly building its own AI agent that browses, codes and works across apps
meldungen.text:
Apple is developing an agentic assistant capable of browsing the web, moving between apps, writing code and calling services, according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg and since removed. The company was seeking an engineer to lead the effort, working with its Siri, UI Frameworks and Apple Foundation Models teams. "These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way," the listing said.

Apple is late to this race. Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots, Anthropic's Duet and Google's Tasks already compete in the field, and Muse, ChatGPT and Perplexity can take control of a Mac through their desktop apps; Google has just started letting Gemini do the same. Apple began rolling out its upgraded Siri in September, which can answer questions about what is on screen and act across apps, and the forthcoming iOS 27.3 update opens Siri integration to "all apps" in a developer preview. Markets noticed: analysts cited Apple's agent plans among the worries behind Friday's tech sell-off.

meldungen.titel: Signal blocks screenshots to keep Siri and Gemini out of your chats, calling AI agents an existential threat to privacy
meldungen.text:
Signal, the encrypted messenger, has decided that the operating system itself has become the weak point. From now on the app prevents screenshots inside its chats on iPhones running iOS 27 and on Android, so that the AI assistants built into those systems can no longer read messages off the screen. In a blog post, its president, Meredith Whittaker, describes OS-level agents as "increasingly hostile to privacy" and as an existential threat to Signal's ability to guarantee confidentiality on its own.

The mechanics differ by platform. On iOS 27 the block targets Siri's "Onscreen Awareness", which captures the open app as an image in order to produce summaries. On Android, Signal switches on its "Screen security" setting as soon as it detects an assistant such as Gemini trying to read the display. Users who need screenshots can turn the protection off in the settings, though Whittaker warns that doing so would "potentially expose" their and their contacts' messages to these agents and break the app's privacy guarantees. The Mac is left out: Signal says the available interfaces are designed only for streaming and copy-protected content, so it cannot block reliably there, and advises Mac users to exclude the app from Siri in their system settings. On Windows, Signal has blocked Microsoft's Recall screenshot feature since 2025.

Whittaker concedes that the remedy is incomplete. Agents could still reach app data by other routes, for instance through the device's file system, and on some Android phones Signal cannot reliably detect the assistants at all. Recent reports suggested that Meta's agent Muse was able to read Signal messages via Android's notification permissions and macOS accessibility tools, which Signal likens to a "skeleton key".

The real target is the platform owners. Google, Apple and Microsoft, Whittaker argues, offer developers no straightforward way to restrict AI access without drastically degrading the user experience. Signal is calling for a documented opt-out from agent access and for accurate information about how the agents actually process data. "Signal is the canary in the coal mine," she writes. Apple counters that its AI features run on the device or in its sealed Private Cloud Compute; Signal replies that confidential computing is no complete answer. Even so, this is not trench warfare: Signal says it is "cautiously optimistic" that Apple and Google are engaging, and Apple has reportedly already closed the macOS accessibility route.

The move had been trailed. In the summer, at TechBBQ in Copenhagen, Whittaker warned that if the trend continued, Signal would be unable to keep its privacy promises within a year or two.

meldungen.titel: Google builds a counterfeit internet to teach its AI agents not to be fooled
meldungen.text:
When AI agents browse on your behalf, gathering information, filling in forms and completing purchases, every web page they read is a potential trap. The most insidious is prompt injection: instructions hidden on a site that hijack an agent and steer it away from its task, for instance into leaking confidential user data or taking actions nobody asked for. To find such weaknesses before attackers do, Google has built what it calls the "Mirror Dimension", a test environment sealed off from the real web and populated with thousands of artificial websites.

Testing on the open internet was never an option, because an agent under test might trigger real transactions. The harder problem was realism. AI models sometimes notice when they are being tested and change their behaviour accordingly; an odd web address or an unconvincing page can give the game away. Google's answer is an elaborate illusion. The agent types genuine addresses such as youtube.com, but Chrome runs in an isolated sandbox whose entire network traffic is diverted to a local proxy server, which serves synthetic versions of the sites instead. So that Chrome does not block the diversion as a security breach, Google installed its own certificate authority as trusted in the test browser, allowing the proxy to issue matching HTTPS certificates.

The fake sites are themselves built by agents: a research agent works out the requirements, a developer agent writes the code, and further agents review the result and suggest improvements. Manipulated content is then planted throughout, hidden in text, images and other page elements. According to Google, the automated pipeline produces more than 1,000 candidate attack tests per security engineer per day, over 30 times what manual work achieves. Wired reports that the environment is to be opened to other teams inside the company.

The approach has clear limits. It defends agents against manipulation by hostile websites, but does nothing about criminals deploying agents as weapons in their own right. And the immediate beneficiary is Google itself, since the environment was designed for Chrome's browser agents: the company has described its method publicly but has not announced plans to share the infrastructure with other browser makers.

meldungen.titel: Deutsche Telekom puts 100 million euros into Mistral AI, its first step towards a strategic partnership
meldungen.text:
Deutsche Telekom is buying into Europe's leading home-grown AI developer. According to Der Spiegel, the group's venture arm, the T.Capital Tech Fund, invested 100 million euros in Paris-based Mistral AI as part of its most recent financing round. Telekom described the stake as a first step towards a future strategic partnership; neither side has published terms beyond the headline figure.

Mistral's latest round on record is its Series D, announced in September: 3 billion euros at a valuation of more than 21 billion, led by Samsung and joined by the Scaleup Europe Fund among others, the largest equity round a European tech company has ever raised. Measured against that, Telekom's ticket is modest. Its significance is strategic rather than financial: Europe's largest telecoms operator is aligning itself with the model maker that European governments, including Austria's federal computing centre, increasingly treat as the sovereign alternative to American labs. The news landed on the day of Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, a reminder of the gulf in scale between Europe's champion and the Claude maker.

meldungen.titel: Anthropic ends its first day worth 1.75 trillion dollars, but the early euphoria halves and Asian markets slump
meldungen.text:
The champagne went a little flat. Anthropic's shares closed their first day on Nasdaq at 97.17 dollars, 17 % above the 83-dollar offer price. That is respectable by any normal standard, but at the first trade the premium had been twice as large. On a fully diluted basis, counting options and employee stock plans, the close values the maker of Claude at about 1.75 trillion dollars; counting only shares outstanding, the market value was about 1.28 trillion.

The day's shape told the story. The first trade did not happen until more than two hours after the opening bell, at 111.50 dollars. Minutes later the stock touched an intraday high of nearly 115 dollars, then slid to 92.72 by early afternoon before recovering slightly. Around 830 million shares changed hands, almost as many as Anthropic sold in the offering. At its peak the fully diluted valuation briefly reached about 2 trillion dollars, nudging Anthropic past SpaceX, which was valued at roughly 1.92 trillion before its own June listing and closed its debut up 19 %, a slightly better first day.

None of this alters the headline fact: at 81.3 billion dollars raised, this is the largest IPO in history. "This technology needs you, not your trust, not your use, but your voice," co-founder Daniela Amodei said as she rang the opening bell.

Outside, the message was different. Activists gathered in Times Square under the banner "Stop Tech Oligarchs", organised by the Stop Funding Billionaires campaign with groups including Climate Defiance and Sunrise NYC. Police arrested four people after repeated warnings. Their central worry was pension money: that index funds, endowments and retirement schemes will buy the stock and absorb the losses if an AI bubble bursts. They also cited job losses, the power and water use of data centres and military applications, and called for a freeze on AI development. Anthropic has not commented.

Markets in Asia drew their own conclusion. With the opening gains melting away and no spark for the wider tech sector, Tokyo's Nikkei fell 4.2 % on Friday to 56,951 points and the broader Topix lost 3.0 %. Shanghai dropped 1.6 %. Fears of new US export controls on AI chips added to the selling.

Update, Friday morning: the full picture of Thursday is grim. The Nasdaq Composite lost 2.3 % to its lowest close since mid April, the S&P 500 fell 2 % for a sixth straight loss, and the Dow shed about 1,100 points to close below 50,000 for the first time since June; AMD dropped 7.7 %. In Asia the Kospi and the Nikkei ended more than 5 % lower, and Taiwan's main index closed its worst week since 1991, down almost 18 %. Anthropic itself slipped almost 5 % after hours but stayed more than 11 % above its offer price. "Normally, the biggest IPOs are done at the peak of the market, not at the bottom," Hao Hong of Lotus Asset Management told the Financial Times; Lombard Odier's John Woods reads it instead as a rotation from chip suppliers towards AI software makers.

Update, Friday evening: the pop lasted one day. About an hour into Friday's session the stock was down 11.4 % at 86.11 dollars, only some 4 % above the offer price, shrinking the fully diluted valuation to about 1.56 trillion dollars. The underwriters exercised the greenshoe option for 147 million extra shares, adding roughly 12.2 billion dollars and lifting IPO proceeds to about 93.5 billion (119.5 billion including a 26-billion private placement); that also removes the banks' built-in price support. Cathie Wood's ARK bought 90.8 million dollars' worth, and history offers some comfort: Facebook and Uber also lost 11 % on their second days.

meldungen.titel: "Kipppunkt": Austria unveils an AI agenda with 15 fields of action, but the actual strategy will not arrive until 2027
meldungen.text:
While Anthropic was being valued at around 2 trillion dollars in New York, Austria's state secretary for digitalisation, Alexander Pröll (ÖVP), declared a "tipping point" in Vienna. Under that title, "Kipppunkt", he presented an AI agenda with 15 fields of action and three goals: Austria should remain capable of acting, prosperous and humane. "At a tipping point, doing nothing is also a decision," he said. It is not yet a strategy. The agenda now goes to public consultation, the input will be evaluated in spring, and the coordinated AI strategy is due in the first half of 2027. It is meant to replace the "AI Mission Austria 2030", written in 2021, before ChatGPT existed.

The government highlighted six proposals. On computing power, a European Community for Computing Power modelled on the old Coal and Steel Community, plus a national roadmap for "small, green, decentralised" data centres whose waste heat could warm schools. With Germany, Austria wants to bring TikTok Europe into European hands. Chancellor Christian Stocker wants an international AI centre under the UN umbrella in Vienna. For the economy, a national mission on physical AI and support for EU Inc and the savings and investments union. Under the heading "education of the heart" comes a social media ban for children under 14 and screen-free primary schools on a "calculator principle". Finally, a constitutional objective in the spirit of Kant: technological progress must serve people.

Much of this is familiar, and none of it has a budget figure yet. Austria had offered up to 1.75 billion euros for an EU AI gigafactory before withdrawing its bid. More concrete progress is happening inside government: under the Public AI banner, the federal computing centre is building tools for civil servants on open-weights Mistral models running on its own servers. Pröll had also written to the European Commission in the summer suggesting the EU try to lure Anthropic to Europe; nothing came of it.

The Greens criticised the process from the start. Their digital spokesman, Süleyman Zorba, complained of "no plan, no structure" and pointed to unfinished business: the EU AI Act required member states to designate a market surveillance authority by August 2025, and Austria has so far only set up an advisory AI service desk at the regulator RTR. Anyone can contribute to the consultation at kipppunkt.gv.at.

Update, Friday: within a day the row was about authorship, not content. FPÖ leader Herbert Kickl, citing a quick check by plagiarism hunter Stefan Weber with the detector Pangram (67 % AI), called the paper "amateurish". Pröll's office simply agreed: "Yes, of course we used AI for it", adding that the imprint now says so. Detectors give probabilities, not proof; one recently rated a page of Thomas Mann's "The Magic Mountain" 60 % AI. Consultation contributions will be evaluated in spring 2027.

meldungen.titel: When Anthropic lands in your ETF: Nasdaq-100 entry expected on 21 December, MSCI may move faster
meldungen.text:
If you own a broad equity ETF, you will soon own a sliver of Anthropic without lifting a finger. The question is only when, and how much. According to Bloomberg, Anthropic is on track to join the Nasdaq-100 at the open on Monday, 21 December, at which point every fund tracking the index will have to buy the shares. The mechanism is Nasdaq's fast-entry rule: a large newcomer can be added after about 15 trading days rather than waiting for the annual reshuffle, and Nasdaq announces the addition after the tenth day of trading. One estimate puts the total passive buying from index inclusions, including the Russell 1000, at around 19 billion dollars.

For European savers the more relevant index is the MSCI World. MSCI also has a fast-entry rule, under which a sufficiently large IPO can be included shortly after its debut. Germany's consumer testing foundation Stiftung Warentest writes that MSCI will now check whether Anthropic qualifies, and that in the fastest case it could be in the indices as early as 1 December. Once that happens, MSCI World ETFs must integrate the stock into their portfolios.

The weighting will be modest at first. Index providers weight by free float, the shares actually available to trade, and only a fraction of Anthropic's equity was sold in the offering; justETF's analysis of the big AI and space listings assumes a free float of around 10 % for companies of this kind, which keeps the starting weight small even for a company valued above a trillion dollars.

That automatic buying is precisely what protesters outside Nasdaq objected to on Thursday. Their fear is that pension funds and index trackers will absorb losses if AI valuations collapse. The crypto outlet Decrypt noted, however, that no rule forces pension funds to buy the shares; it is index funds that follow mechanically.

meldungen.titel: ChatGPT now transcribes as you speak, and the ten-minute dictation limit is gone
meldungen.text:
OpenAI has rolled out Live Dictation, which transcribes voice prompts in real time rather than waiting until you stop recording. It is available globally on every ChatGPT plan, on the web, the desktop app and the iOS and Android apps. While dictating, you can tap the audio waveform to see the live transcript and then edit it in the prompt box before sending.

OpenAI has also scrapped the ten-minute cap on voice dictation and says the feature is now more reliable. It follows this year's overhaul of the two-way voice mode. A separate "record mode" for transcribing meetings and voice notes remains in beta and is limited to paid workspaces, but the ordinary dictation box can already turn a voice message into bullet points.

meldungen.titel: Google's homepage gets a sidebar for your AI chats
meldungen.text:
The single search box that defined Google for a quarter of a century is getting company. A collapsible sidebar on the homepage now lists the searches you have run in AI Mode, lets you continue those threads, search them, start new ones or connect a Gemini Notebook. Robby Stein, Google's vice president of product, said people increasingly come to Search with questions "that aren't just one and done", and that in testing the sidebar "made a big difference" in helping them keep exploring. It is rolling out globally on desktop.

It is the latest step in a steady redesign: the AI Mode button arrived in the search bar last year, and in May the box was enlarged for longer queries and given AI-powered autocomplete. Search is becoming a conversation you return to rather than a query you fire off.

meldungen.titel: Dutch data protection authority warns against AI glasses after one claimed to have called an ambulance it never called
meldungen.text:
The Dutch data protection authority, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after testing six models. The concern is no longer only that wearers can film others unnoticed, which the regulator already warned in September is almost always unlawful. The AI itself proved unreliable.

In one simulated emergency, a tester asked the glasses for help with resuscitation. The device replied that it had alerted the emergency number 112 and that an ambulance was on its way. It had called no one; the reassurance was a hallucination. In other tests the glasses gave dating advice to an adult expressing interest in children, and misread medicine leaflets and safety warnings on toys. "A pair of glasses that films you without your knowledge is already worrying. A pair that also gives wrong advice in life-threatening situations clearly goes too far," said deputy chair Monique Verdier.

The AP did not name products, but according to Reuters, glasses from Meta, TCL/RayNeo, Rokid and HTC are on sale in the Netherlands. The regulator cannot ban sales, which is a matter for product safety authorities, though it may gain powers under the EU AI Act. Norway plans temporary bans on AI glasses in selected places.

meldungen.titel: Bitcoin slides to a four-month low near 61,000 dollars as record ETF outflows follow the Anthropic listing
meldungen.text:
Anyone who expected money to flow back into crypto once Anthropic's offering was done has been disappointed. Bitcoin fell to about 61,300 dollars overnight, its lowest level since early July, and traded around 61,600 dollars (roughly 55,300 euros) on Friday morning: down just over 3 % in a day, 9 % on the week and almost 30 % from its late September high of about 87,000. It is heading for a seventh consecutive weekly loss; only in 2022 did such a streak run longer. Ethereum has slipped below 1,750 dollars, and the whole crypto market is now worth about 2.13 trillion dollars.

The main pressure comes from exchange-traded funds. On the day of the listing, about 582 million dollars left US spot Bitcoin ETFs, 541 million of it from BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust alone, its largest daily outflow since launch. November's outflows now total about 3.5 billion dollars. Forced liquidations of roughly 700 million dollars in 24 hours, overwhelmingly bets on rising prices, added to the selling, as did Fed minutes showing nearly all officials expect further rate rises before the December decision.

Whether Anthropic actually drained money from crypto is disputed: outflows accelerated after the debut rather than reversing, which, as Decrypt notes, points to a broad retreat from risk rather than a targeted rotation. Technically the picture has darkened with a "death cross", and Bitfinex warns of a fall to the July low of about 57,800 dollars if outflows persist; an RSI near 20, deeply oversold, is the only argument for a bounce.

meldungen.titel: Nvidia nearly 40 % below its peak despite record revenue, as the Huang scandal unsettles investors
meldungen.text:
On paper, Nvidia has just delivered a blockbuster quarter. Third-quarter revenue more than doubled year on year to 115.8 billion dollars, data centre revenue rose 110 %, and nearly 20 billion dollars came from the new Vera Rubin platform, which interim chief executive Colette Kress called the "fastest product ramp in company history". "We've got this," she told investors on Tuesday. By Thursday the shares were hovering around 150 dollars, close to 40 % below their all-time high of 6 October, and a brief post-earnings rise had evaporated, even as Wall Street paid up for Anthropic, one of Nvidia's biggest customers.

The slide has two layers. First came a broad sell-off in chip stocks on AI-bubble fears. Then the leadership crisis. On 29 October The New York Times reported that US intelligence believed co-founder Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese espionage plot involving his relationship with an executive at a Singapore data centre client. The market barely reacted at first. On 5 November, after midterm results raised fears that new Democratic governors could slow data centre construction, the stock fell 9.2 %, its worst day in at least a year. On 8 November Huang apologised to staff in a memo for an extramarital affair as the board opened an independent investigation; reports of a second alleged affair followed. His departure was announced on 12 November, sending the shares down nearly 14 % at the open to an intraday low of 148.80 dollars, the lowest in a year.

The new chairman, Harvey Jones, told investors the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO" and has hired a search firm, even though Huang posted that he would be "honoured" to return. Huang will appear before three House committees on 1 December for transcribed interviews, with Nvidia's general counsel following on 2 December.

Update, Friday: the pressure is now spreading to the states. California's attorney general, Rob Bonta, has served Nvidia with a formal list of questions to establish whether powerful chips or confidential information reached China and whether the company misled investors and the public; Nvidia's conduct "sets off alarm bells", he said. The company did not respond at first. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also urged Nvidia to clarify swiftly who knew what, and when.

meldungen.titel: Vienna's Chatarmin lets ten staff go and hands their work to an in-house AI agent, which it now plans to sell as a company of its own
meldungen.text:
Chatarmin, a bootstrapped Viennese start-up, is cutting its team from 30 to 20 people and will not refill the posts. Their tasks, co-founder and chief executive Johannes Mansbart wrote on LinkedIn, will be taken over by "TorbenAI, our internal A.I. agent system". He insists money is not the motive: the company, he says, is doing better than ever, with 8 million euros in annual recurring revenue after 50 months and no outside investors.

The departures span SEO and GEO (search and AI-answer optimisation), CMS management, customer success and key accounts, sales and go-to-market, as well as operations, HR and back end. The aim is to shrink further, to ten people. Mansbart borrows his maxim from waterdrop co-founder Martin Murray, "as few people for as long as possible", and puts it bluntly: at a young company, anything that can be done without people should be, because people are "simply the most expensive and most inefficient work resource". He described those leaving as highly talented and offered to introduce them to new employers.

TorbenAI is meant to become a business in its own right. According to Mansbart it fully automates SEO and GEO, account management and customer support, and Chatarmin is now offering it to other firms. In January the product will be spun off into a separate vehicle, to which it has already been sold; Mansbart and co-founder Armin Daryabegi will own it entirely through their holding company and fund it, true to form, without venture capital. His stated ambition, posted under the announcement, is "10PAX 100M ARR": ten people generating 100 million in recurring revenue, more than twelve times today's figure, within five years.

Founded in 2022, Chatarmin built its name on WhatsApp marketing and customer service for e-commerce brands, claims more than 500 customers including Marc O'Polo, waterdrop and Holy, and competes with Berlin's charles and Superchat. Mansbart is among the loudest advocates of bootstrapping in Austria's start-up scene and once dismissed venture capital as a "sucker's game".

The case fits a wider pattern: Canva recently cut more than 1,000 jobs, Vienna included, citing AI. Whether the arithmetic holds is contested; Christoph Ott of LEAN-CODERS warns that companies too readily infer from one successful automation that they need fewer people across the board.

meldungen.titel: Goldfish, an AI memory app founded by two Swedes, wins Slush 100 and 500,000 euros without giving up equity
meldungen.text:
It turns out a goldfish has the best memory after all. Goldfish, a San Francisco start-up building a personal AI memory for your computer, won this year's Slush 100, the flagship pitch competition at the Slush tech conference in Helsinki. In Thursday's final on the Founder Stage it beat Britain's Sqwish Labs and Luxembourg's TerraSpark. The prize is 500,000 euros with no equity attached, a first in the competition's history.

The product, for macOS and Windows, keeps track of what you are working on, from emails and Slack messages to Notion pages, documents and open browser tabs, and stores that context in a local database. Press the Option key in any text field and Goldfish drafts a reply, summarises a thread or rewrites a sentence in your own tone and with the relevant background, so there is no need to paste the backstory into a chatbot first. The founders' pitch is that popular models know most of the internet yet almost nothing about the work in front of you; in their words, AI has the memory of a goldfish. On privacy the company relies on local storage with no cloud sync, and users can pause capture, exclude apps or sites and delete their history. Text generation runs through Azure OpenAI with zero data retention, according to a review by Cascade Insights, and a local MCP server lets users pass their captured context to Claude Desktop.

Goldfish was founded by chief executive Joel Edholm and chief technology officer Kaspian Jakobsson, who built it during Entrepreneur First's "The Bridge" residency in San Francisco; both previously worked at Strawberry Browser and the Y Combinator alumnus Depict. Since early access opened in June the app has been used more than a million times, Slush says, and early users include go-to-market teams at ElevenLabs, Deel and Vercel. It is free for now; neither pricing nor funding has been disclosed.

The competition itself drew a record of more than 1,400 applicants, all founded in 2023 or later, at seed stage or earlier, with less than 10 million euros raised. The cheque has shrunk: from 2022 to 2025 the winner received a 1 million euro investment from venture firms. No Austrian start-up made the top 100, which was led by Britain (17), the United States (15), Switzerland (14) and Germany (13). The contrast with Switzerland, which also placed two teams among the 20 semi-finalists, is stark, although Austria was hard to miss in Helsinki with a delegation of around 300.

meldungen.titel: What Anthropic's record IPO means for Austrian start-ups: Speedinvest and AI Austria see a tailwind, but warn of dearer AI
meldungen.text:
Five years after its founding, Anthropic has pulled off the largest stock market flotation in history, raising about 81.3 billion dollars. Its shares closed their first Nasdaq session at 97.17 dollars, some 17 % above the 83-dollar offer price, for a valuation of roughly 1.77 trillion dollars. The Austrian start-up outlet brutkasten asked two of the country's most prominent tech voices what that means closer to home: Oliver Holle, chief executive and managing partner of Speedinvest, Austria's largest venture capital firm, and Clemens Wasner, founder of the association AI Austria and chief executive of enliteAI.

Neither buys the familiar worry that a mega-listing sucks capital and attention away from smaller companies. Holle calls the crowding-out argument wrong: the IPO is "a massive validation of the AI trade", showing investors the returns successful AI firms can generate, which should benefit European scale-ups such as Mistral and Black Forest Labs. He expects higher valuations, but also higher standards. Wasner points to the multiple oversubscription and compares the debut with Google's in 2004, which kicked off a new wave of tech listings.

Both are sober about Austria itself. The country is "simply not comparable" with Silicon Valley, Holle says, least of all as a stock exchange; rather than chasing a record listing in Vienna, it should help exceptional founders succeed globally, after which an IPO follows by itself. Wasner sees the obstacles at European level: no unified capital market, and pension funds that invest far less in venture capital than their American peers. Until that changes he expects more "Delaware flips", in which European start-ups move their corporate structure to the United States, and he is sceptical about the proposed EU Inc. company form.

The sting is in the costs. Wasner recalls that Uber and Slack raised prices markedly after going public in pursuit of profitability, and expects a similar rise in the cost of AI models and subscriptions in the medium term, especially after OpenAI's own listing. On the upside, Anthropic might set up start-up programmes or a venture arm of its own, as Nvidia and Google have done.

meldungen.titel: Google books a Blue Origin rocket to put its AI data centres in orbit by 2029
meldungen.text:
Google has booked a dedicated launch on Blue Origin's heavy-lift New Glenn rocket for Project Suncatcher, its attempt to move AI computing into space. The flight is targeted for the first quarter of 2029, project lead Travis Beals announced, and will place satellites in sun-synchronous orbit, each with roughly the capacity of a data-centre rack. Beals calls the project a "long-term moonshot"; neither company has disclosed the number of satellites or the price.

So far Suncatcher is tiny: a prototype built with Planet flew on a SpaceX rideshare this autumn, carrying four of Google's tensor processing units running the open Gemma model. Two more test satellites next year will check whether the chips can be linked by laser. The logic is the same as at SpaceX, which plans orbital AI data centres from 2028, the start-up Starcloud and Nvidia with its space-grade chips: on the ground, data centres wait years for grid connections and face local opposition, while solar panels in such an orbit can generate up to eight times more power.

The economics remain doubtful. By Google's own reckoning, launch costs must fall below 200 dollars per kilogram by the mid 2030s for orbital computing to compete, and Beals told NPR he does not expect it to become cheaper within five years. Cooling is hard in a vacuum, which limits the prototype to 15 minutes of computing at a time, and New Glenn has flown only a handful of times, misplacing a payload in April.

meldungen.titel: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for 3.7 billion dollars, 70 % below what Intuit paid five years ago
meldungen.text:
The Milan software collector has bagged another classic at a steep discount. Bending Spoons is acquiring the email marketing service Mailchimp from Intuit at an enterprise value of 3.68 billion dollars. Intuit paid about 12 billion in 2021, half in cash and half in stock, when Mailchimp had some 13 million users and 800,000 paying customers. That is a loss of roughly 70 % in five years.

The business has stalled rather than collapsed. In the first quarter of Intuit's 2027 fiscal year, Mailchimp's revenue slipped 1 % to 313 million dollars, and the full year is expected at about 1.26 billion, flat. It is highly profitable, with segment operating income of 202 million, or 65 % of revenue. Intuit, which announced in spring that it would cut about 17 % of jobs and reduce investment in Mailchimp, says the sale sharpens its focus on AI-driven business software and will fund share buybacks. Bending Spoons' chief executive, Luca Ferrari, promised to "invest substantially in the business".

It is Bending Spoons' largest deal yet. Founded in 2013 and listed on Nasdaq since the summer, the company recently bought Airtable and Miro, both far below their former valuations, and in Austria the pet tracker maker Tractive for 770 million euros. Alongside the Mailchimp deal it announced a 1.3 billion dollar private placement, after Berkshire Hathaway invested a further 330 million. In the third quarter, acquisitions lifted revenue 125 % to 780 million dollars, while organic growth was just 3 %; the adjusted operating margin was 54 %.

The playbook is well known: reorganise, rebuild the technology, raise prices. Evernote lost its entire staff, about three quarters of WeTransfer's were to go, and at Tractive in Pasching more than half the jobs were cut. Co-founder Matteo Danieli insists customer retention has remained "remarkably stable". Mailchimp faces stiff competition from Klaviyo, HubSpot and France's Brevo.
